Since [real numbers](Real_number "Real number") can be represented as distances or intervals on a line, the [slide rule](Slide_rule "Slide rule") was invented in the 1620s, shortly after Napier's work, to allow multiplication and division operations to be carried out significantly faster than was previously possible.[[13]](History_of_computing_hardware#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKellsKernBland194392-17) [Edmund Gunter](Edmund_Gunter "Edmund Gunter") built a calculating device with a single logarithmic scale at the [University of Oxford](University_of_Oxford "University of Oxford"). His device greatly simplified arithmetic calculations, including multiplication and division. [William Oughtred](William_Oughtred "William Oughtred") greatly improved this in 1630 with his circular slide rule. He followed this up with the modern slide rule in 1632, essentially a combination of two [Gunter rules](Gunter's_scale "Gunter's scale"), held together with the hands. Slide rules were used by generations of engineers and other mathematically involved professional workers, until the invention of the [pocket calculator](Pocket_calculator "Pocket calculator").[[14]](History_of_computing_hardware#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKellsKernBland194382-18)

### Mechanical calculators

In 1609 [Guidobaldo del Monte](Guidobaldo_del_Monte "Guidobaldo del Monte") made a mechanical multiplier to calculate fractions of a degree. Based on a system of four gears, the rotation of an index on one quadrant corresponds to 60 rotations of another index on an opposite quadrant.[[15]](History_of_computing_hardware#cite_note-19) Thanks to this machine, errors in the calculation of first, second, third and quarter degrees can be avoided. Guidobaldo is the first to document the use of gears for mechanical calculation.

[Wilhelm Schickard](Wilhelm_Schickard "Wilhelm Schickard"), a German [polymath](Polymath "Polymath"), designed a calculating machine in 1623 which combined a mechanized form of Napier's rods with the world's first mechanical adding machine built into the base. Because it made use of a single-tooth gear there were circumstances in which its carry mechanism would jam.[[16]](History_of_computing_hardware#cite_note-20) A fire destroyed at least one of the machines in 1624 and it is believed Schickard was too disheartened to build another.

## First Five Universities that Created Turing-Complete Computers

### 1. University of Pennsylvania (1945-1946)
**ENIAC** (Electronic Numerical Integrator and Computer) - Completed in 1945, formally dedicated at University of Pennsylvania on February 15, 1946. ENIAC was the first programmable, electronic, general-purpose digital computer. It was Turing-complete with conditional branching and was programmable to solve a wide range of numerical problems through reprogramming. Built at the Moore School of Electrical Engineering.

### 2. University of Manchester (1948)
**Manchester Baby** (Small-Scale Experimental Machine) - Ran its first program on June 21, 1948. It was the first electronic stored-program computer built at the University of Manchester by Frederic C. Williams, Tom Kilburn, and Geoff Tootill. It was the first working machine to contain all the elements essential to a modern electronic digital computer.

### 3. University of Cambridge (1949)
**EDSAC** (Electronic Delay Storage Automatic Calculator) - First ran on May 6, 1949, at the University of Cambridge Mathematical Laboratory. Built by Maurice Wilkes and his team, it was the first practical stored-program electronic computer and provided a computing service to Cambridge University until 1958.

### 4. University of Illinois (1952)
**ORDVAC** (Ordnance Discrete Variable Automatic Computer) - Passed acceptance tests on March 6, 1952, at Aberdeen Proving Ground. Built by the University of Illinois, it was one of the first computers to have a compiler. The university also built **ILLIAC I** which became operational on September 1, 1952 - both were stored-program computers based on the IAS architecture.

### 5. Institute for Advanced Study/Princeton (1952)
**IAS Machine** (sometimes called the von Neumann machine) - Became operational on June 10, 1952. This was the first electronic computer built at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, New Jersey, under the direction of John von Neumann. While IAS is technically separate from Princeton University, it's located in Princeton and von Neumann held positions at both institutions, making it closely associated with Princeton University.

These five institutions were pioneers in computer science, with the first Turing-complete computers being built at universities between 1945 and 1952. It's worth noting that many other early computers (like Colossus, Harvard Mark I, Z3) were built but either lacked conditional branching or weren't Turing-complete at the time.
